title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Warren hits the brakes on new data centers for a year amid power and water worries.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Tuesday, September 8, and yesterday Warren became the latest community to put the brakes on new data center proposals.
Exactly, Graham. The city council there approved a full 12-month moratorium, and that feels like part of a bigger pattern we're seeing across southeast Michigan.
Let's unpack the Warren decision first and then zoom out to what it means for electric bills, water supplies, and towns trying to keep some say over these massive projects.
Why did Warren act now? Residents in Macomb County have been sounding alarms about how these facilities pull huge amounts of power and water.
Right. The council voted for the year-long pause specifically to give officials time to study and update zoning rules before any large facilities move forward.
So it's not a permanent ban, just a timeout. How does that fit with what's happening in other places?
It's part of a wave. We've seen similar moves in Ypsilanti, Kalamazoo, Garfield Township, and Lakeshore, all trying to slow things down while they figure out the impacts.
What are the main concerns residents keep raising? Is it mostly the power draw or the water use for cooling?
Both, plus the strain on local roads, potential noise, and questions about whether the tax revenue and jobs are worth losing farmland or stressing the grid.
And how does that affect electric bills for regular folks 30 or 60 miles away?

When big new demand hits the regional grid, utilities often pass costs along through higher rates or need expensive upgrades. That's why communities farther out are watching these local decisions closely.
Who are the main players here? Developers pushing these projects, or local officials responding to neighbors?
It's both. Developers see Michigan's data center opportunity with AI growth, while residents and township boards are pushing back on fast approvals without enough study.
What's the history of these fights? Have we seen this scale of pushback before?
Not at this level. The last couple years brought a surge of proposals, and now more than a handful of communities have enacted or extended pauses to write better rules.
What happens next in Warren? Do they have a timeline for new zoning?
The 12 months give them breathing room to draft standards on size, power, water, and location. If they don't act, the moratorium lifts automatically.
And could a successful recall effort elsewhere change the math, like the one targeting the Springfield Township supervisor?
Absolutely. Those recalls show data centers are now election issues, and a shift in local leadership can flip approvals or tighten rules fast.
How about water specifically? These places use a lot for cooling, right?
Yes, and in areas already watching aquifer levels or competing with farms and homes, that daily usage adds up quickly.
Farmland is another angle. Are we talking about prime ag land being converted?
In several proposals yes, which raises long-term food production and open-space questions for rural townships.
So the Warren pause is really a signal that local control is back on the table?
That's the read. Communities want time to weigh the trade-offs instead of rushing into multibillion-dollar projects.
All right, let's move to quick hits. Starting with that recall push in Springfield Township.

Residents there are gathering signatures to oust the supervisor they say fast-tracked data centers that could strain roads, power, and water. A successful recall would change who controls future approvals.
Ypsilanti is extending its freeze too.
Yes, the city council kept the moratorium in place while it studies power and water impacts. That could ripple into regional electricity rates if projects get approved later.
Over in Saline Township they delayed a vote on a big tax break for Oracle.
Supervisors postponed action on the 12-year abatement request. Residents are questioning whether the forgone revenue for roads and schools matches the promised jobs.
A developer is restarting a bid at the old Emerson Electric site.
That project would bring new power demand and tax questions to the community, with nearby residents feeling effects on rates and land use.
Mason County actually broke ground on two major centers.
Western Mason County approved construction. Those will draw significant electricity and create construction and operations jobs, but locals will see impacts on reliability and taxes.
Kalamazoo added a moratorium to its zoning code.
Officials are writing a temporary ban into the rules as AI proposals multiply, giving time to study while fewer projects compete for power and land.
Garfield Township is taking a full year to craft rules.
Supervisors there will spend 12 months on zoning and permitting standards, which could limit power demand, noise, and water use in Grand Traverse County.
Mid-Michigan residents got a town hall look at the numbers.
A university-hosted session laid out concrete megawatt and daily water demands so people within 30 miles could ask questions before projects advance.
And Lakeshore Township is using existing zoning to block them.
Officials say current ordinances already keep large server farms away from homes and wells, so water and noise impacts stay off the table for now.
Now let's look at what's on deck for listeners who want to show up.
Tonight, September 8, Ypsilanti City Council has the second reading and possible adoption of its 60-day emergency moratorium on data center zoning permits.
Tomorrow, September 9, the City of Ionia is holding an informational meeting on the data center industry and potential impacts.
Also on the ninth, University of Michigan is hosting a community town hall on the proposed $1.2 billion high-performance computing facility in Ypsilanti Township.
And on September 15, Ypsilanti City Council has a public hearing on the zoning ordinance text amendment and the 60-day emergency moratorium.
Those are the real meetings where people can weigh in.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Warren's Year-Long Data Center Pause Sparks Broader Michigan Debate on Power, Water and Lo
